Sampling depth, NOPE, and energy distance

GW McElfresh

2026-10-20

Source: vignettes/sampling-depth.Rmd
sampling-depth.Rmd

Sequencing depth should set the precision of a composition estimate and leave the meaning of a summary statistic alone. Two of the package’s headline quantities, PPGT1 and the between/within ratio RR, break that rule. PPGT1 is the posterior probability that RR exceeds 1. As depth grows, the Dirichlet posterior collapses onto the sample RR. Groups that do not differ still yield a sample RR that is rarely exactly 1, so PPGT1 drifts toward 0 or 1. RR also puts within-group spread in its denominator, so one composition shift yields a large RR in homogeneous cohorts and a small one in heterogeneous cohorts. Here, we use a simulation study to show when the Null-Oriented Permutation Equivalence (NOPE) intervals and the energy distance (EE, energyDistance) give a better-calibrated answer than PPGT1 and RR, and when they cost power. A NOPE is a permutation-calibrated null reference interval for a conditional effect (R_PPGTnope on RR and E_PPGTnope on EE). It shares the goal of a permutation test, but it reports a region instead of a p-value

The simulation design

Each simulated cohort has two groups of 8 subjects and 10 categories. The internal helper simulate_composition_cohort() separates the three sources of variation we care about:

  • Depth. reads_per_subject sets the multinomial count total, and with it the count noise within each subject.
  • Heterogeneity. Each subject draws a latent composition from a Dirichlet centered on its group’s mean; concentration sets how tightly subjects cluster (larger is more homogeneous).
  • Shift. shift moves composition mass from the most abundant category to the rarest one in the second group only. A shift of 0.05 is a 5-point change in composition.

The helper also returns the latent compositions, so we can compute a noise-free reference RR and EE for any cohort and measure what count noise does to each statistic.

library(HellingerDistanceEnrichment)

cohort <- HellingerDistanceEnrichment:::simulate_composition_cohort(
  n_subjects_per_group = 8,
  n_categories = 10,
  reads_per_subject = 2000,
  concentration = 50,
  shift = 0,
  seed = 1
)
head(cohort$long_table)
#>     subjectId  category   group   n
#> 1 Control_S01 Category0 Control 260
#> 2 Control_S02 Category0 Control 185
#> 3 Control_S03 Category0 Control 462
#> 4 Control_S04 Category0 Control 250

We start with a single cohort with no shift to show the problem in miniature. We use fewer posterior draws and shuffles than the defaults to keep the vignette fast.

demo_result <- CompareGroupCompositions(
  cohort$long_table,
  method = "bayes",
  contrasts = c("Control", "Treatment"),
  nPosterior = 50,
  nNopeShuffles = 100,
  seed = 2
)
demo_result$omnibus[c("effectSize", "PPGT1", "R_PPGTnope", "R_nopeHigh", "energyDistance", "E_PPGTnope", "E_nopeHigh")]

This cohort gives PPGT1 = 0.90 and R_PPGTnope = 0.00, with E_PPGTnope = 0.00. One cohort proves little either way. The scenarios below use 100 to 200 cohorts per condition from a precomputed grid.

Running the full grid

We ran about 800 Bayes cohorts at the package defaults (nPosterior = 100, nNopeShuffles = 200). That took about 35 minutes on five cores, which is too slow for a vignette. The script data-raw/simulate_sampling_study.R in the source repository runs it once and saves per-cohort summaries to inst/extdata/sampling_study.rds. Each cohort gets its seed from a fixed formula that we set before the first run. We did not tune any seed toward an outcome. The saved file records which code produced it:

study_path <- system.file("extdata", "sampling_study.rds", package = "HellingerDistanceEnrichment")
sampling_study <- readRDS(study_path)
str(sampling_study$metadata[c("packageVersion", "gitDescribe", "generatedOn")])
#> List of 3
#>  $ packageVersion: chr "0.1.0"
#>  $ gitDescribe   : chr "cab7c93-dirty"
#>  $ generatedOn   : chr "2026-10-09"
str(sampling_study$metadata$settings)
#> List of 7
#>  $ subjectsPerGroup : num 8
#>  $ nCategories      : num 10
#>  $ nPosterior       : num 100
#>  $ nNopeShuffles    : num 200
#>  $ nPermutations    : num 999
#>  $ priorPseudocounts: num 0.5
#>  $ seedFormula      : chr "1e6 * scenario + 1e3 * cell + replicate"

If gitDescribe lags far behind the installed package, rerun the script before trusting the numbers below.

summarize_rate <- function(hits) {
  rate <- mean(hits, na.rm = TRUE)
  n_cohorts <- sum(!is.na(hits))
  c(rate = rate, se = sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n_cohorts))
}

# Okabe-Ito hues, validated for color-vision separation; each keeps one meaning
# throughout this vignette.
rule_colors <- c(
  "PPGT1 > 0.95" = "#0072B2",
  "R_PPGTnope > 0.95" = "#D55E00",
  "permutation p < 0.05" = "#009E73"
)
statistic_colors <- c("R (excess over 1)" = "#0072B2", "E" = "#D55E00")

Scenario 1: false positives and power across depth

We simulated 100 cohorts at each of three depths (50, 500, and 2000 reads per subject), once with no shift and once with a 5-point shift, at a moderate concentration of 50. For each cohort we recorded three decisions: PPGT1 > 0.95, R_PPGTnope > 0.95, and a permutation p-value below 0.05 from 999 label shuffles. We use the permutation test as the anchor, because its false-positive rate should sit near 5% at every depth.

nope_calibration <- sampling_study$nopeCalibration
rule_hits <- list(
  "PPGT1 > 0.95" = nope_calibration$PPGT1 > 0.95,
  "R_PPGTnope > 0.95" = nope_calibration$R_PPGTnope > 0.95,
  "permutation p < 0.05" = nope_calibration$pValue < 0.05
)
nope_cells <- split(
  seq_len(nrow(nope_calibration)),
  list(nope_calibration$shift, nope_calibration$readsPerSubject),
  drop = TRUE
)
nope_rates <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(rule_hits), function(rule_name) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(nope_cells, function(row_idx) {
    rate <- summarize_rate(rule_hits[[rule_name]][row_idx])
    data.frame(
      rule = rule_name,
      shift = nope_calibration$shift[row_idx[1]],
      readsPerSubject = nope_calibration$readsPerSubject[row_idx[1]],
      rate = rate[["rate"]],
      se = rate[["se"]]
    )
  }))
}))
rownames(nope_rates) <- NULL
nope_rates$arm <- ifelse(nope_rates$shift == 0, "No shift (false positives)", "5-point shift (power)")
nope_rates$rule <- factor(nope_rates$rule, levels = names(rule_colors))

rate_at <- function(rule_name, shift_value, reads) {
  row <- nope_rates[nope_rates$rule == rule_name & nope_rates$shift == shift_value &
                      nope_rates$readsPerSubject == reads, ]
  sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * row$rate)
}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(nope_rates, aes(x = factor(readsPerSubject), y = rate, color = rule, group = rule)) +
  geom_hline(
    data = data.frame(arm = "No shift (false positives)", rate = 0.05),
    aes(yintercept = rate),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray50"
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6, position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)) +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(ymin = pmax(0, rate - 2 * se), ymax = pmin(1, rate + 2 * se)),
    size = 0.3,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(arm, levels = c("No shift (false positives)", "5-point shift (power)"))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = rule_colors, name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = function(x) paste0(100 * x, "%")) +
  labs(x = "Reads per subject", y = "Cohorts flagged") +
  egg::theme_article() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

Share of cohorts flagged by each decision rule, with two standard errors. The dashed line marks 5%.

With no shift, PPGT1 > 0.95 flagged 1% of cohorts at 50 reads per subject but 25% at 500 and 27% at 2000. The permutation test held near 5% at every depth (4%, 6%, 4%). R_PPGTnope > 0.95 never exceeded 1%, so NOPE holds its false-positive rate at the depths where PPGT1 loses it.

That calibration costs power. With a 5-point shift at 2000 reads, the permutation test detected 86% of cohorts and R_PPGTnope > 0.95 detected 70%. At 50 reads per subject the gap widens to 50% versus 1%. Dirichlet noise at shallow depth pulls every draw’s RR toward 1, while the shuffled edge stays near 1.06. The 0.95 threshold is strict: nearly every posterior draw must clear its own 95th shuffle percentile, the equivalent of a significant shuffle test in 95% of draws.

nope_half <- aggregate(
  cbind(flagged = R_PPGTnope > 0.5) ~ shift + readsPerSubject,
  data = nope_calibration,
  FUN = mean
)
nope_half
#>   shift readsPerSubject flagged
#> 1  0.00              50    0.01
#> 2  0.05              50    0.27
#> 3  0.00             500    0.06
#> 4  0.05             500    0.69
#> 5  0.00            2000    0.04
#> 6  0.05            2000    0.85

A looser reading, R_PPGTnope > 0.5, flags a cohort when a typical draw clears its shuffle edge. In this grid it flagged 4% of null cohorts and 85% of shifted cohorts at 2000 reads, close to the permutation test. The package reports the posterior probability and leaves the threshold to you. Pick one that matches your tolerance for false positives. Take heed that R_PPGTnope > 0.95 sits at the conservative end.

The NOPE on EE uses the same shuffles, so we recorded E_PPGTnope for every cohort as well.

summarize_rule <- function(hits) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(hits, na.rm = TRUE))
nope_by_statistic <- do.call(rbind, lapply(nope_cells, function(row_idx) {
  cell <- nope_calibration[row_idx, ]
  data.frame(
    shift = cell$shift[1],
    readsPerSubject = cell$readsPerSubject[1],
    R_PPGTnope_95 = summarize_rule(cell$R_PPGTnope > 0.95),
    E_PPGTnope_95 = summarize_rule(cell$E_PPGTnope > 0.95),
    R_PPGTnope_50 = summarize_rule(cell$R_PPGTnope > 0.5),
    E_PPGTnope_50 = summarize_rule(cell$E_PPGTnope > 0.5),
    permutation_05 = summarize_rule(cell$pValue < 0.05),
    medianE_nopeHigh = signif(stats::median(cell$E_nopeHigh), 2)
  )
}))
rownames(nope_by_statistic) <- NULL
nope_by_statistic
#>   shift readsPerSubject R_PPGTnope_95 E_PPGTnope_95 R_PPGTnope_50 E_PPGTnope_50
#> 1  0.00              50            0%            0%            1%            1%
#> 2  0.05              50            1%            1%           27%           29%
#> 3  0.00             500            0%            1%            6%            5%
#> 4  0.05             500           45%           43%           69%           69%
#> 5  0.00            2000            1%            1%            4%            4%
#> 6  0.05            2000           70%           70%           85%           85%
#>   permutation_05 medianE_nopeHigh
#> 1             4%           0.0250
#> 2            50%           0.0260
#> 3             6%           0.0110
#> 4            69%           0.0130
#> 5             4%           0.0098
#> 6            86%           0.0120

energy_rate_at <- function(threshold, shift_value, reads) {
  cell <- nope_calibration[nope_calibration$shift == shift_value & nope_calibration$readsPerSubject == reads, ]
  sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(cell$E_PPGTnope > threshold, na.rm = TRUE))
}
energy_edge_at <- function(reads) {
  signif(stats::median(nope_calibration$E_nopeHigh[nope_calibration$readsPerSubject == reads]), 2)
}

E_PPGTnope tracks R_PPGTnope in this grid. With no shift, E_PPGTnope > 0.95 flagged at most 1% of cohorts at any depth. With a 5-point shift it detected 70% of cohorts at 2000 reads and 43% at 500. The edge itself moves with depth. Its median fell from 0.025 at 50 reads per subject to 0.011 at 2000; shallow count noise likely widens the spread of EE across shuffles. Across all six cells, the two NOPEs reached the same decision at 0.95 in 98% of cohorts. These cohorts differ only by a shift in mean composition, which moves RR and EE together. Scenario 5, where groups differ in spread, is where the two part.

Scenario 2: depth and the size of each statistic

We held each cohort’s latent compositions fixed, changed the number of reads drawn from each subject, and measured how much of the true effect each statistic kept. We drew 200 cohorts with a 5-point shift, computed RR and EE on the latent compositions as a noise-free reference, then resampled counts at eight depths from 25 to 5000 reads per subject. For RR we track the excess over 1, because 1 is its no-difference value. For EE, 0 is the no-difference value, so we track EE itself.

depth_drift <- sampling_study$depthDrift
depth_drift$rRetained <- (depth_drift$effectSize - 1) / (depth_drift$referenceEffectSize - 1)
depth_drift$eRetained <- depth_drift$energyDistance / depth_drift$referenceEnergyDistance

summarize_retained <- function(values, statistic_label, reads) {
  data.frame(
    statistic = statistic_label,
    readsPerSubject = reads,
    median = stats::median(values),
    lower = stats::quantile(values, 0.25, names = FALSE),
    upper = stats::quantile(values, 0.75, names = FALSE)
  )
}
depth_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(depth_drift, depth_drift$readsPerSubject), function(cell) {
  rbind(
    summarize_retained(cell$rRetained, "R (excess over 1)", cell$readsPerSubject[1]),
    summarize_retained(cell$eRetained, "E", cell$readsPerSubject[1])
  )
}))
rownames(depth_summary) <- NULL
depth_summary$statistic <- factor(depth_summary$statistic, levels = names(statistic_colors))

retained_at <- function(statistic_label, reads) {
  sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * depth_summary$median[depth_summary$statistic == statistic_label &
                                                 depth_summary$readsPerSubject == reads])
}
ggplot(depth_summary, aes(x = readsPerSubject, y = median, color = statistic)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper, fill = statistic), alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = sort(unique(depth_summary$readsPerSubject))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(100 * x, "%")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = statistic_colors, name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = statistic_colors, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Reads per subject (log scale)", y = "Noise-free effect retained") +
  egg::theme_article() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

Share of the noise-free effect each statistic keeps as depth falls (median and interquartile range over 200 cohorts).

Both statistics shrink at shallow depth, and EE shrinks less. At 50 reads per subject the excess of RR keeps 37% of its noise-free value while EE keeps 57%. By 500 reads they reach 90% and 96%. The two shrink for different reasons. Count noise adds to between- and within-group distances alike, which pulls RR toward 1. With squared distances that noise cancels from EE in expectation. EE still shrinks because Jeffreys softening pulls every shallow composition toward uniform, and because the square root of a noisy proportion is biased downward. Take heed of the wide interquartile range for EE at 25 and 50 reads: EE is less biased than RR at shallow depth, but no more precise.

Scenario 3: the same shift in groups of different spread

We held the shift at 5 points and the depth at 2000 reads, and varied each group’s concentration on its own over 10, 30, 100, 300, and 1000. The 25 cells cover equally homogeneous groups, equally heterogeneous groups, and every mix where one group is more variable than the other, as when a disease arm scatters more than control. Each cell holds 100 cohorts.

heterogeneity <- sampling_study$heterogeneity
cell_medians <- aggregate(
  cbind(effectSize, energyDistance) ~ controlConcentration + treatmentConcentration,
  data = heterogeneity,
  FUN = stats::median
)
reference_cell <- cell_medians$controlConcentration == 1000 & cell_medians$treatmentConcentration == 1000
relative_values <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    statistic = "R (excess over 1)",
    relative = (cell_medians$effectSize - 1) / (cell_medians$effectSize[reference_cell] - 1)
  ),
  data.frame(
    statistic = "E",
    relative = cell_medians$energyDistance / cell_medians$energyDistance[reference_cell]
  )
)
relative_values$statistic <- factor(relative_values$statistic, levels = names(statistic_colors))

fold_range <- function(statistic_label) {
  values <- relative_values$relative[relative_values$statistic == statistic_label]
  sprintf("%.1f", max(values) / min(values))
}
ggplot(relative_values, aes(x = statistic, y = relative, color = statistic)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8, position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_color_manual(values = statistic_colors, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Relative to concentration 1000 in both groups (log scale)") +
  egg::theme_article()

Median of each statistic in the 25 spread combinations, relative to the most homogeneous cell. Every cell uses the same 5-point shift.

The same 5-point shift gave a median RR anywhere from 1.04 to 2.02 across these cells, a 28.4-fold range in the excess over 1, because RR divides by within-group spread. EE moved over a 2.5-fold range. If you compared these cohorts by RR, you would report a shift that grew and shrank with group spread although we never changed it. We suspect the square root’s curvature explains the residual movement in EE. When subjects scatter widely around their group mean, the mean of their square-root compositions falls. A shift toward a rare category likely interacts with that curvature.

round(tapply(
  heterogeneity$pValue < 0.05,
  list(control = heterogeneity$controlConcentration, treatment = heterogeneity$treatmentConcentration),
  mean
), 2)
#>        treatment
#> control   10   30  100 300 1000
#>    10   0.22 0.75 1.00   1    1
#>    30   0.57 0.53 0.96   1    1
#>    100  1.00 0.95 0.99   1    1
#>    300  1.00 1.00 1.00   1    1
#>    1000 1.00 1.00 1.00   1    1

The permutation test on RR detected the shift in nearly every cell except where both groups were heterogeneous (concentration 10 or 30 in both), where power fell as low as 22%. Heterogeneity lowers power here, and the p-value is the place to report that loss.

Scenario 4: ranking contrasts

Ranking pairwise contrasts by effect size is a common next step after an omnibus test. Spread in the denominator does the most damage there. We built three contrasts per replicate in which the largest shift sits in the most heterogeneous groups and the smallest in the most homogeneous ones: a 2-point shift at concentration 1000, a 5-point shift at 100, and an 8-point shift at 20. Each replicate includes all three. We count how often each statistic orders them by their true shift.

ranking <- sampling_study$ranking
ranking$contrastLabel <- factor(
  ranking$contrastLabel,
  levels = c("small shift, homogeneous", "medium shift, moderate", "large shift, heterogeneous")
)
orders_by_shift <- function(values, shifts) all(diff(values[order(shifts)]) > 0)
by_replicate <- split(ranking, ranking$replicate)
r_correct <- mean(vapply(by_replicate, function(d) orders_by_shift(d$effectSize, d$shift), logical(1)))
e_correct <- mean(vapply(by_replicate, function(d) orders_by_shift(d$energyDistance, d$shift), logical(1)))
r_inverted <- mean(vapply(by_replicate, function(d) {
  d$effectSize[d$shift == 0.02] > d$effectSize[d$shift == 0.08]
}, logical(1)))

aggregate(cbind(effectSize, energyDistance) ~ contrastLabel, data = ranking, FUN = stats::median)
#>                contrastLabel effectSize energyDistance
#> 1   small shift, homogeneous   1.282585    0.004165164
#> 2     medium shift, moderate   1.210152    0.021277407
#> 3 large shift, heterogeneous   1.111942    0.045250209
ranking_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(contrastLabel = ranking$contrastLabel, statistic = "R", value = ranking$effectSize),
  data.frame(contrastLabel = ranking$contrastLabel, statistic = "E", value = ranking$energyDistance)
)
ranking_long$statistic <- factor(ranking_long$statistic, levels = c("R", "E"))

ggplot(ranking_long, aes(x = contrastLabel, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.size = 0.8, color = "gray30", fill = "gray90") +
  facet_wrap(~ statistic, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) sub(", ", "\n", x)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  egg::theme_article()

R and E across the three contrasts, ordered by true shift (200 replicates).

EE ordered the three contrasts by their true shift in 84% of replicates; RR did so in 2%. RR placed the 2-point shift in homogeneous groups above the 8-point shift in heterogeneous groups in 94% of replicates. RR answers a different question correctly here: relative to its spread, the small homogeneous shift is the more separable one. RR misleads when you use it to ask which contrast moved composition the most.

Scenario 5: a difference in spread with no shift

We next isolate a spread difference from a mean shift, the one case where RR and EE disagree by design. Both groups share one mean composition, but the treatment group scatters more than control (concentration 15 versus 200). We include a matched arm with equal spread (200 versus 200) as the baseline. Each arm holds 100 cohorts at 2000 reads per subject.

spread_only <- sampling_study$spreadOnly
spread_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(spread_only, spread_only$treatmentConcentration), function(arm) {
  data.frame(
    treatmentConcentration = arm$treatmentConcentration[1],
    medianR = stats::median(arm$effectSize),
    medianE = stats::median(arm$energyDistance),
    permutationFlagged = mean(arm$pValue < 0.05),
    ppgtnopeFlagged = mean(arm$R_PPGTnope > 0.95),
    energyNopeFlagged = mean(arm$E_PPGTnope > 0.95)
  )
}))
rownames(spread_summary) <- NULL
spread_summary
#>   treatmentConcentration   medianR       medianE permutationFlagged
#> 1                     15 1.1481730  0.0043386735               1.00
#> 2                    200 0.9919977 -0.0003266425               0.02
#>   ppgtnopeFlagged energyNopeFlagged
#> 1            0.99              0.09
#> 2            0.00              0.00
shifted_e <- stats::median(nope_calibration$energyDistance[nope_calibration$shift == 0.05 &
                                                              nope_calibration$readsPerSubject == 2000])
spread_e <- spread_summary$medianE[spread_summary$treatmentConcentration == 15]

A spread difference alone pushed RR to a median of 1.15. Both the permutation test (100%) and R_PPGTnope > 0.95 (99%) flagged nearly every cohort, while E_PPGTnope > 0.95 flagged 9%. Pairwise Hellinger distances between a tight group and a scattered group tend to exceed the average of the two within-group distances. The ratio therefore rises above 1 even though the centroids coincide. EE moved to a median of 0.0043, about 20% of the median EE for a 5-point shift at the same depth.

Your question sets which behavior you want. If a change in subject-to-subject variability is the biology of interest, RR and its tests detect it and EE barely moves. If the question is whether mean composition shifted, a significant R_PPGTnope here is a true statement about the distance distributions but a misleading answer about composition. EE near 0 is the warning sign. When you read the two together, a large RR or R_PPGTnope beside an EE near 0 and a low E_PPGTnope marks a spread difference.

Choosing a quantity

Situation Favored quantity
Deep sampling, deciding whether groups differ R_PPGTnope, E_PPGTnope, or the permutation p-value; not PPGT1
Shallow sampling or small shifts, deciding whether groups differ Permutation p-value; NOPE probabilities > 0.95 lose power
Reporting effect size across depths or studies E (shrinks less than R)
Groups with different or unequal spread E
Ranking contrasts E
Spread differs but mean composition does not R and R_PPGTnope detect it; E and E_PPGTnope stay low

Split the work between the quantities. Decide with the label-shuffling machinery, either the permutation p-value or the NOPE probabilities. Those methods hold their false-positive rate as depth grows; PPGT1 does not. Pick E_PPGTnope when the question is whether mean composition shifted, and R_PPGTnope when a difference in spread also counts. Describe the size of the effect with EE, because it keeps its meaning across depth, heterogeneity, and contrasts better than RR does. Keep RR in view as well: a large RR beside a small EE is the signature of a spread difference. We simulated one family of cohorts (8 versus 8 subjects, 10 categories, a shift into the rarest category). The exact percentages will move with your design. The direction of each comparison follows from the mechanisms above, so we expect it to hold.
